Abstract:
Abstract Objectives: The objective of this study was the evaluation of the professional exposure to nanoparticles during tasks performed in workstations for production of metallic parts by laser welding additive manufacturing. Materials and methods: The study was developed in an installed additive manufacturing machine, having controlled temperature and humidity in an industrial unit where metal parts were being produced using stainless steel powders of granulometry of 10 to 35 μm. Results and discussion: Monitoring of airborne nanoparticles emission was made using adequate equipment, which showed considerable number of nanoparticles over the baseline, having the same composition as the steel powder used. Conclusion: It is concluded that the values of professional exposure to nanoparticles are high in these workstations and that the nanoparticles to which the workers are exposed are small in size (around 15 nm), thus having a strong capacity for alveolar penetration and, consequently, with a strong possibility of passing to the bloodstream, accumulating in the body.

URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/jres.126.013, doi:10.6028/jres.126.013. This article has 26 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt explains that a two-colour pyrometer calculates a ratio temperature from the relative emitted intensities at two wavelengths. This is not necessarily the true thermodynamic temperature: it depends on assumptions about the target’s spectral emissivity, commonly a wavelength-independent graybody assumption, and on calibration. Two-colour measurements can tolerate emissivity changes or optical-path losses when those effects influence both wavelengths equally, but their uncertainty is difficult to establish without independent reference data. The excerpt does not specifically determine whether the measured temperature corresponds to the vapour-depression wall temperature. It instead warns that LPBF process by-products—including hot metal vapour, condensate, and ejecta—can emit, absorb, reflect, and refract radiation before it reaches the detector. Consequently, the pyrometer reading may be influenced by radiation from or attenuation through these by-products rather than solely by the depression wall. Their contribution varies with laser power, scan velocity, material properties, oxygen content, and shielding-gas velocity, creating process-dependent measurement uncertainty. The provided text does not report the specific trend of ratio temperature versus scan speed and power; it only indicates that these parameters can change by-product effects and therefore potentially alter pyrometry readings.

The excerpt identifies several limitations and potential failure mechanisms in coaxial LPBF melt-pool monitoring. Internal back-reflections in the imaging chain can generate bright artifacts and interfere with interpretation of the melt-pool signal; coherent coaxial illumination can additionally produce speckle formation. Signal-processing leakage can cause errors in identifying melt-pool oscillation frequencies, particularly when neighboring spectral peaks lie within the narrow bandwidth of the power-spectral-density estimate. The text also contrasts coaxial/Lagrangian observation with fixed off-axis observation: coaxial monitoring uses a moving observation frame and therefore removes acquisition-time constraints associated with a fixed viewpoint, while frequency resolution remains governed by the observed scan-vector length, with Δfres,PD = v/lobs. The excerpt does not explicitly discuss scan-angle-dependent signal vignetting, ghost reflections, back-reflection into the process laser, thermal drift of dichroic filters, or emissivity changes caused by oxide formation on aluminum. Nor does it provide a specific scan-angle correction algorithm. Its relevant design guidance is to use coaxial illumination for more uniform illumination and lower power consumption, while recognizing internal reflections and speckle as disadvantages; off-axis illumination is easier to set up but may suffer from nonuniform illumination and requires high intensity over a large area.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The metal additive manufacturing industry has experienced significant advancement and growth over the past decades. Powder bed fusion stands out as a promising technology for industries such as aerospace and biomedical due to its ability to produce complex geometries with short lead times. A critical drawback of the technology is the potential for defects to arise, restricting full adoption by these highly regulated industries. Achieving process control remains challenging due to many interacting process variables, coupled with stochastic deviations which can result in defects. While these defects may be detected using ex-situ techniques, this is usually a very costly step. Hence, a critical challenge is the need for in-situ detection of defects to improve quality assurance. Despite the variety of in-situ sensors and defect detection algorithms that are emerging in commercial machines, detection accuracy and efficacy remain problematic. These sensors generate large, complex datasets that traditional pattern detection methods struggle to interpret. This presents an excellent opportunity for machine learning, which can uncover complex patterns in large volumes of multi-modal data. This paper offers a critical review of the current state-of-the-art with respect to in-situ monitoring of the powder bed fusion process. It includes a general overview of the various defect types, as well as analysis of different sensing techniques. Special emphasis is placed on the types of machine learning models employed and the methods used to generate their training data. Key breakthroughs are highlighted, and actionable recommendations are provided for future research and areas of improvement.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Reliable process monitoring is critical for advancing laser powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M), as it provides the process information required for corrective control actions to prevent defects such as lack-of-fusion and keyhole porosity. A promising approach for PBF-LB/M process monitoring is coaxial measurement of light emitted from the meltpool area. More than two hundred research studies on coaxial monitoring of the meltpool have been performed, but there is still no validated and reliable method for measuring a suitable variable that could be directly used as an input for high-resolution control of the PBF-LB/M process, enabling process parameters such as laser power and scan speed to be dynamically adjusted not only at the part level, but locally for individual micrometer-scale segments along the scan track. This work reviews existing research studies on coaxial meltpool monitoring and identifies potential future research and development directions toward a standard and reliable meltpool monitoring method. Meltpool depth is identified as a particularly promising control-relevant variable. With the ability to monitor and control meltpool depth, it is possible to avoid undesirable process conditions due to too high or too low energy input, which would result in defects like keyhole porosity or lack-of-fusion. However, only five studies have attempted to estimate the melt pool depth coaxially during the PBF-LB/M process. Despite these attempts, there is no sufficiently validated method for high-resolution coaxial monitoring of meltpool depth in PBF-LB/M. The potential solution seems to be in combining concepts and recent discoveries from two-color coaxial camera- and photodiode-based meltpool area monitoring approaches. Based on the existing literature and hands-on experiences with establishing and working with coaxial monitoring systems, this work also provides guidelines and lists the most common challenges for implementing coaxial monitoring of the meltpool in the PBF-LB/M process.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Continuous innovations in welding and additive manufacturing (AM) technologies have introduced challenges related to process stability and uncertainties in ensuring high quality. Given the high complexity and transient nature of these processes, effective online acoustic monitoring is crucial for ensuring manufacturing quality and improving processing efficiency. This paper first elucidates the principles of acoustic signal generation in welding and additive manufacturing. It then provides a comprehensive review of the application of acoustic methods for quality monitoring in these processes, covering both structural acoustic emission (AE) and airborne acoustic monitoring techniques. Finally, it summarizes the current challenges and issues faced by acoustic monitoring technologies in welding and additive manufacturing and outlines potential future development directions.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In the present work, the recent advancements in additive manufacturing (AM) techniques for fabricating nanocomposite parts with complex shaped structures are explained, along with defect non-destructive testing (NDT) methods. A brief overview of the AM processes for nanocomposites is presented, grouped by the type of feedstock used in each technology. This work also reviews the defects in nanocomposites that can affect the quality of the final product. Additionally, a detailed description of X-CT, ultrasonic phased array technology, and infrared thermography is provided, highlighting their potential application in non-destructive inspection of nanocomposites in the future. Lastly, it concludes by offering recommendations for the development of NDT methods specifically tailored for nanocomposites, emphasizing the need to utilize NDT methods for optimizing nano-additive manufacturing process parameters, developing new NDT techniques, and enhancing the resolution of existing NDT methods.

Abstract:
In the last decade, the filter community has innovated both design techniques and the technology used for practical implementation. In design, the philosophy has become “if you can't avoid it, use it”, a very practical engineering approach. Modes previously deemed spurious are intentionally used to create in-line networks incorporating real or imaginary transmission zeros and also reduce the number of components and thus further miniaturize; spurious responses are re-routed to increase the passband width or stopband width, frequency variation in couplings is used to create complex transfer functions, with all of these developments using what was previously avoided. Clever implementations of baluns into passive and active networks is resulting in a new generation of noise-immune filters for 5G and beyond. Finally, the use of a diakoptic approach to synthesis has appeared an evolving approach in which small blocks (“singlets”, “doublets”, etc.) are cascaded to implement larger networks, (reducing the need for very complex synthesis), with this new approach promising a large impact on the implementation of practical structures. Filter technology has migrated towards “observe it and then adapt it”, pragmatically repurposing tools not specifically originally intended for the applications. Combinations of surface wave and bulk wave resonators with L-C networks are improving the loss characteristics of filters in the region below 2 GHz. Lightweight alloys and other materials designed for spacecraft are being used in filters intended for space, to provide temperature stability without the use of heavy alloys such as Invar. Fully-enclosed waveguide is being replaced in some cases by planar and quasiplanar structures propagating quasi-waveguide modes. ## pqac-00000017

From text 'brandau2022angulardependenceof pages 8-9'.

Benedikt Brandau, Torsten Mai, Frank Brueckner, and Alexander F. H. Kaplan. Angular dependence of coaxial and quasi-coaxial monitoring systems for process radiation analysis in laser materials processing. Optics and Lasers in Engineering, 155:107050, Aug 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.optlaseng.2022.107050, doi:10.1016/j.optlaseng.2022.107050. This article has 13 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt indicates a strong angular and scan-position dependence in coaxial LPBF monitoring. As beam or field tilt increases, the measured spectral intensity decreases. At the maximum tested beam tilt of 18.5°, the coaxial measurement retained only 30.2% of the intensity measured near the reference position, implying a substantial galvo-angle-dependent signal loss. The F-theta lens contributes through both longitudinal and transverse chromatic aberration: because it is not apochromatic, different wavelengths are focused at different axial positions, increasing the effective integration zone and reducing the contribution of unfocused wavelengths. Across the scan field, the shorter-wavelength (blue) component has a shorter focal length, so at larger field angles the monitoring point can move away from the interaction zone; the shorter-wavelength spectral integral consequently decreases. At nonzero material and beam tilt, projection also enlarges the focus spot and lowers laser intensity, although the excerpt identifies chromatic aberration as the more important influence. A quasi-coaxial arrangement using a second scanner and reflective mirror optics avoids wavelength-dependent transmission errors. Its field-dependent spot-size and numerical-aperture variations are corrected using a white-light reference measurement and a 100-μm optical fiber scanned across the processing field, reducing the remaining intensity deviation to a maximum of 1.8%.

## pqac-00000018

From text 'brandau2022angulardependenceof pages 13-13'.

Benedikt Brandau, Torsten Mai, Frank Brueckner, and Alexander F. H. Kaplan. Angular dependence of coaxial and quasi-coaxial monitoring systems for process radiation analysis in laser materials processing. Optics and Lasers in Engineering, 155:107050, Aug 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.optlaseng.2022.107050, doi:10.1016/j.optlaseng.2022.107050. This article has 13 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

In LPBF, the coaxial monitoring signal is strongly position-dependent because the scan position changes the laser/workpiece incidence angle through the F-theta scanning optics. Signal intensity decreases as the galvo angle and distance from the scan-field center increase. Across the working field, the uncorrected spectral intensity falls by approximately 36% for solid samples and 51% for powder-coated samples, with the larger powder decrease attributed to stronger angle-dependent effects. The F-theta lens also introduces chromatic aberration in the coaxial optical path: short-wavelength components below 510 nm are not detected even at a scanner-mirror angle of 5°. The reported angular dependence is associated with changes in spot size and interaction-zone geometry, as well as the field-dependent numerical aperture and process-radiation geometry. A reflective quasi-coaxial setup avoids the severe short-wave loss and records the process signal accurately. For solid materials, field measurements can be normalized using correction factors incorporating the measuring channel’s numerical aperture and laser intensity distribution over the working field. The correction can adjust the overall spectral intensity, but it cannot independently restore individual atomic emission peaks; residual deviations arise from setup geometry and the field-dependent emission angle.

The excerpt shows a strong angular and scan-position dependence of coaxial LPBF monitoring intensity. Conventional coaxial measurements across the scan field are considered unreliable, primarily because optical chromatic aberrations and angle-dependent transmission alter the recorded signal. At the largest tested beam or galvo tilt of 18.5°, the solid-sample signal falls to 30.2% of the normal-incidence value, while the powder signal falls to 44.0%. Across spectra, deviations are about 7.5% at 4.9° AOI and reach 44% at 18.5°. The process-radiation intensity itself also decreases with AOI. The laser spot intensity changes by approximately 4.9% for material tilt and 6.5% for beam tilt over the tested angular range; the difference between these two cases reaches 3.3% at 18.5°. The F-theta lens contributes angle-dependent transmission losses and field-dependent spot size, ellipticity, and focus-plane curvature. In the optical analysis, the lens transmission weakening and changing spot area were included when calculating relative spot intensity. An apochromatized F-theta lens is suggested as a possible optical remedy for coaxial chromatic errors, while quasi-coaxial monitoring avoids the dominant chromatic problem. The excerpt indicates that coaxial monitoring intensity depends on scan position and trajectory because the meltpool and its thermal tail change their orientation and position relative to the coaxial sensor’s field of view. During straight scanning, the emitting region has a relatively stable geometry, but during sharp scan-direction changes—especially 180° turnarounds—the scan velocity and direction change rapidly. This changes the fraction of the meltpool and heated surroundings captured by the sensor. A meltpool tail that is partly outside the effective measurement field during straight scanning may contribute differently during a turnaround, producing intensity changes unrelated to actual meltpool-depth or energy-input changes. Therefore, cumulative coaxial emission intensity has a geometric/angular dependence and may be ambiguous during transient scan paths. However, the provided excerpt does not quantify the signal variation as a function of galvo angle, does not discuss the optical effect of an f-theta lens, and does not identify specific corrections or calibration formulas applied to compensate for these effects. The excerpt does not provide a numerical signal variation, percentage, or direct galvo-angle calibration, so the magnitude of the change cannot be determined from these pages alone. For pre-objective scanning, the F-theta lens is central to the optical behavior. F-theta lenses provide field flattening, high numerical aperture, possible telecentricity, and stable passive optics, but their imaging errors and optical properties can affect the monitoring result. Coaxial systems also suffer from scanner/lens-related imaging effects, while quasi-coaxial systems experience deviations from variable process zones and changing observation angles. The authors create a model for the emitted plasma radiation and use it to correct measured values. ## pqac-00000031

From text 'brown2024atmosphereeffectsin pages 2-5'.

Ben Brown, Cody Lough, Davis Wilson, Joseph Newkirk, and Frank Liou. Atmosphere effects in laser powder bed fusion: a review. Nov 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17225549, doi:10.3390/ma17225549. This article has 19 citations.

The excerpt describes plume or metal-vapour attenuation in LPBF as the reduction in laser energy delivered to the melt pool when metal vapour and surrounding cover gas interact with the laser beam. The vapour and gas can become ionized, forming a plasma plume above the melt pool. Attenuation occurs through three principal mechanisms: inverse bremsstrahlung absorption, in which electrons and photons interact; Rayleigh scattering by plume particles; and refraction, which increases the beam’s effective spot size. The extent of these interactions depends on laser wavelength and power, as well as the ionization energies of the metal vapour and cover gas. Metal vapours are more readily ionized than common cover gases, with listed ionization energies of 7.9 eV for iron, 6.8 eV for titanium, and 6.0 eV for aluminum. The excerpt does not provide a measured percentage of laser power lost specifically to plume absorption and scattering, nor does it report direct beam-attenuation measurements. The percentages stated concern melt-pool coupling rather than plume loss: conduction-mode melting typically absorbs less than 30% of incident laser energy, while keyhole-mode melting can absorb as much as 90% because of repeated absorption within the depression. Therefore, these values should not be interpreted as the percentage lost to plume attenuation.

Abstract:
Challenge 3 of the 2022 NIST additive manufacturing benchmark (AM Bench) experiments asked modelers to submit predictions for solid cooling rate, liquid cooling rate, time above melt, and melt pool geometry for single and multiple track laser powder bed fusion process using moving lasers. An in-house developed A dditive M anufacturing C omputational F luid D ynamics code (AM-CFD) combined with a cylindrical heat source is implemented to accurately predict these experiments. Heuristic heat source calibration is proposed relating volumetric energy density (ψ) based on experiments available in the literature. The parameters of the heat source of the computational model are initially calibrated based on a Higher Order Proper Generalized Decomposition- (HOPGD) based surrogate model. The prediction using the calibrated heat source agrees quantitatively with NIST measurements for different process conditions (laser spot diameter, laser power, and scan speed). A scaling law based on keyhole formation is also utilized in calibrating the parameters of the cylindrical heat source and predicting the challenge experiments. In addition, an improvement on the heat source model is proposed to relate the Volumetric Energy Density (VED_σ) to the melt pool aspect ratio. The model shows further improvement in the prediction of the experimental measurements for the melt pool, including cases at higher VED_σ. Overall, it is concluded that the appropriate selection of laser heat source parameterization scheme along with the heat source model is crucial in the accurate prediction of melt pool geometry and thermal measurements while bypassing the expensive computational simulations that consider increased physics equations.

{"answer": "## Critical Review of In-Situ Monitoring Design for a Lab-Built LPBF Machine Processing Aluminium Alloys

### (a) Findings Compared with Published Measurements and Practice

**Melt-pool regime and size.** The operating point of 320 W with a 96 µm spot gives P_L/d_b ≈ 3333 W/mm. Leis et al. mapped the AlSi10Mg process window and placed the optimum at P_L/d_b = 3000–3500 W/mm, corresponding to "key-bowl melting" (KBM)—an intermediate regime between heat-conduction melting (HCM, aspect ratio <0.7) and deep-penetration melting (DPM, aspect ratio >1.4) (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000064). The KBM regime features a shallow vapour depression with an aspect ratio near unity—consistent with the design's claim that tracks remain conduction-shaped up to ~350 W while surface boiling begins from ~200 W. The model's calibrated absorptivity of 0.35 sits between the literature values for aluminium alloy conduction-mode absorptivity (~0.15) and transition-mode absorptivity (~0.425), and is therefore physically reasonable for the shallow-depression/KBM regime (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000043). Patel and Vlasea further noted that aluminium alloys have a narrow conduction-to-keyhole transition window because of their high reflectivity, low surface tension at boiling (~0.28 N/m), and volatile Mg content, so the boundary is sensitive to small perturbations in power or focus (pqac-00000005). The modelled pool dimensions (~324 × 208 µm at 25 °C, ~405 × 260 µm at 200 °C) could not be directly validated against the retrieved literature, which reports aspect ratios and cross-sectional areas rather than absolute widths at this exact parameter set. However, the trend of wider pools at elevated preheat is well established, and the simulated width/depth ratios fall in the expected HCM-to-KBM range.

**Two-colour pyrometer reading.** The design's finding that a 700/900 nm ratio pyrometer reads ~2570 K, nearly independent of speed and preheat, is qualitatively consistent with published pyrometry behaviour in LPBF. Gutknecht et al. demonstrated that the two-colour ratio temperature in LPBF can be misleading: near an overhang where excessive energy was physically present, the ratio temperature paradoxically decreased, and would have driven a feedback controller in the wrong direction (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000041). The ratio is not simply the vapour-depression wall temperature. Deisenroth et al. at NIST showed that hot metal vapour, condensate, and ejecta can emit, absorb, reflect, and refract radiation before it reaches the detector, with plume contributions biasing a solidification-temperature measurement by approximately 45 °C (16 °C standard uncertainty) even for well-characterized high-purity nickel (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000009). The design's interpretation that the ratio reads the "depression wall" is therefore an oversimplification. Rather, the signal is a radiance-weighted average over the spatially integrated field of view, dominated by the hottest emitting surface (likely the depression interior), but contaminated by plume emission and selective spectral attenuation. The near-independence from speed and preheat is consistent with the pyrometer being dominated by a hot region whose temperature is set by the boiling point and cavity geometry rather than by bulk thermal conditions—but published evidence cautions that this invariance can break down with changes in plume density, oxide state, or scanning geometry. No published two-colour pyrometry study specifically for aluminium LPBF at these wavelengths was found, so the 2570 K value remains an unvalidated model prediction.

**Silicon camera blindness to Al solidification.** The claim that a 12-bit silicon camera at 850–970 nm cannot see the Al mushy zone (750–925 K, i.e., 477–652 °C) is well supported. Taminger et al. found that a silicon/NIR camera operating at 0.875–1.05 µm was configured for approximately 700–2200 °C and was unsuitable for aluminium's lower temperature range; an InGaAs SWIR camera was specifically required and was calibrated over 300–1000 °C (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055). Boone calibrated a silicon camera with an 850 nm long-pass filter over 600–825 °C (pqac-00000056). These observations confirm that silicon detectors at NIR wavelengths have practical detection thresholds around 600–700 °C for metallic surfaces with low emissivity, placing the Al mushy zone at or below the detection limit. The design's InGaAs channel at 1.55 µm extending sensitivity to ~800 K is therefore a well-motivated addition.

**Spatter reaching cover slides.** The literature confirms that spatter and vapour condensate contaminate optics and powder beds in LPBF (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000032). However, no published study was found that quantifies the fraction of spatter droplets reaching a cover slide at a specific height, so the design's modelled 1.5–5 % fraction reaching a slide 126 mm above the plate is a machine-specific CFD prediction that cannot be directly validated against literature values. The qualitative finding that cross-flow removes most airborne spatter and condensate is consistent with published studies showing that stronger, more uniform gas flow improves spatter removal and reduces redeposition (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

**Thermophoretic deposition.** The design's prediction that a window 10 K colder than the gas collects 20–120× more condensate via thermophoresis is physically plausible but was not found in the LPBF-specific literature. Thermophoresis is well documented in aerosol science and welding fume contexts, but quantitative LPBF window-contamination studies with controlled temperature differentials were not retrieved.

**Plume attenuation.** The design's modelled 0.05–0.2 % beam attenuation appears significantly lower than published measurements. Brown et al. reviewed laser welding plume attenuation and reported total attenuation values of 11–23 % at atmospheric pressure for Yb-fibre laser welding, decreasing to ~2 % at reduced pressures around 3 kPa (pqac-00000035). The dominant mechanism for 1 µm lasers is Rayleigh scattering by ultra-fine condensate particles rather than inverse bremsstrahlung absorption (pqac-00000034). The design's value of 0.05–0.2 % may be reasonable for the aluminium LPBF case at modest power (320 W) with effective cross-flow removing fume, but it is 1–2 orders of magnitude lower than the welding measurements at atmospheric pressure and should be treated as an optimistic lower bound. The discrepancy may partly reflect the difference between welding (continuous deep keyhole, dense plume) and shallow-depression LPBF with active cross-flow, but the design should acknowledge this tension.

### (b) Failure Modes Not Addressed in the Design

**1. Scan-angle-dependent coaxial signal (vignetting and chromatic aberration).** This is the most critical omission. Brandau et al. demonstrated that coaxial monitoring intensity through an F-theta lens dropped by 36 % on solid samples and 51 % on powder-coated samples across the scan field, with only 30.2 % of the reference intensity remaining at 18.5° beam tilt (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019). The Thorlabs FTH160-1064 f-theta lens is designed for 1064 nm laser delivery, not for broadband monitoring. Chromatic aberration shifts the focal position for shorter wavelengths, so the 680–720 nm and 880–920 nm pyrometer bands may have different field-dependent collection efficiencies—corrupting the two-colour ratio spatially across the build plate. Without per-band, per-position calibration, the photodiode pyrometer data will contain systematic spatial errors that could exceed real process variations. A quasi-coaxial approach using reflective optics reduced residual deviation to 1.8 % (pqac-00000017).

**2. Ghost reflections and back-reflections.** Caprio et al. identified internal back-reflections in the coaxial imaging chain as a source of bright artifacts (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000049). The DMSP1000 short-pass dichroic at 45° can produce ghost images from its second surface reflection. At 1070 nm, even 0.1 % leakage of the 500 W process laser through the dichroic yields 0.5 W—enough to saturate or damage the monitoring detectors. The design mentions a "shared short-pass 1070 nm blocker" but does not specify its OD or whether wedged optics are used to prevent retro-reflection. Inserting a beam splitter into the optical path can laterally displace or angle the transmitted laser beam, requiring careful alignment (pqac-00000051).

**3. Thermal drift of dichroics and filters.** The design does not discuss temperature-induced spectral shifts of the dichroic edge positions. Thin-film interference coatings typically shift ~0.01–0.02 nm/°C, so a 50 °C temperature rise in the scan head could shift a dichroic edge by 0.5–1 nm. While this is small relative to the pyrometer band widths, it could matter for the narrow stop-band avoidance of the 750–875 nm galvo-mirror coating region.

**4. Emissivity changes with oxide formation on aluminium.** Aluminium's emissivity can change dramatically with surface oxidation. The design processes four different alloys (AlSi10Mg, 6061, 7075, grain-refined variants) that will produce different oxide layers on solidified tracks. Published NIST measurements showed nickel emissivity varying from 0.39 (virgin surface) to 0.33 (solidified tracks) (pqac-00000009). For aluminium alloys, which form tenacious oxide layers rapidly, the variation is expected to be larger and alloy-dependent. This will affect both the camera signal interpretation and the two-colour pyrometer ratio.

**5. EMI from galvo and servo drives.** The PicoScope 4444 digitizing photodiodes and AE signals at ≥2 MS/s is susceptible to electromagnetic interference from the galvo drivers, which switch currents at high frequencies. The design does not mention shielding, differential sensing, or galvo-synchronous noise characterization. Published monitoring reviews note EMI as a concern for sensitive AE and photodiode measurements in LPBF environments.

**6. AE noise from the recoater and gas loop.** Seleznev et al. found that the inert-gas circulation pump increased AE noise amplitude from approximately 0.2 V to 2 V—a tenfold increase that persisted throughout the build (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059). The design routes the AE signal through a waveguide down a hollow piston rod, which may act as a mechanical antenna for vibrations from the recoater drive, the piston servo, and the gas-flow system. The design specifies keeping the preamp at or below 65 °C but does not address these mechanical noise sources.

**7. Data volume and real-time processing.** At 500 fps cropped, the IMX296 camera generates roughly 0.5–1 GB/min; photodiodes at ≥2 MS/s produce ~16 MB/min per channel; AE at 2 MS/s adds another ~16 MB/min. For multi-hour alloy screening builds, total data volumes can reach hundreds of gigabytes. The design does not describe a data reduction, feature extraction, or storage strategy. Published reviews emphasize that data volume is a major practical barrier to LPBF monitoring implementation (pqac-00000024).

**8. Calibration drift.** The design does not describe a periodic recalibration protocol. Cover-slide contamination, dichroic thermal drift, and AE coupling degradation will cause progressive signal changes that could be mistaken for process variation. Lane et al. at NIST emphasized the importance of reference measurements and uncertainty quantification for LPBF monitoring (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007).

### (c) Five Biggest Risks and Cheapest Retirement Experiments

The following table ranks the five highest risks to obtaining useful data from this monitoring design, with quantitative evidence and the most cost-effective experiment to retire each risk.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Discussion of risk ranking rationale:**

Risk 1 (scan-angle dependence) is ranked highest because it affects every coaxial measurement channel continuously and cannot be corrected post-hoc without a spatial calibration. The measured 36–51 % signal variation across the field (pqac-00000018) exceeds many process signatures of interest, which are typically 10–30 % changes in photodiode intensity. For the two-colour pyrometer, differential chromatic aberration between 700 nm and 900 nm through the f-theta lens could corrupt the ratio itself, not just its amplitude, making flat-field correction insufficient without per-band calibration.

Risk 2 (pyrometer misinterpretation) is ranked second because the design explicitly interprets the ~2570 K ratio as a physical temperature of the depression wall. Published evidence shows this interpretation can be qualitatively wrong—the ratio moved in the opposite direction to true energy input near an overhang (pqac-00000039)—and that plume emission biases even well-calibrated single-wavelength measurements by tens of degrees (pqac-00000009). For aluminium, where the plume contains volatile Mg and potentially Na/K with strong atomic emission lines, spectral contamination of the pyrometer bands is a particular concern.

Risk 3 (AE noise) is ranked third because the gas-loop pump noise was measured at 10× the baseline, potentially burying crack signals from hot-cracking-susceptible alloys like 7075 (pqac-00000058). The waveguide coupling adds unknown transfer-function modifications.

Risk 4 (window contamination) is ranked fourth because it creates a time-dependent systematic error that affects all coaxial channels simultaneously but at different rates depending on wavelength-dependent scattering by condensate particles.

Risk 5 (Si camera blindness) is ranked fifth because while confirmed by literature (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000055), the design already acknowledges this limitation and proposes the InGaAs channel as mitigation. The risk is that the InGaAs channel may be deferred as "optional," leaving the Si camera as the only imaging sensor, in which case solidification monitoring for the Al alloys would be impossible.

### Summary of Key Quantitative Comparisons

| Design Claim | Literature Value | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Absorptivity 0.35 | Conduction ~0.15, transition ~0.425, keyhole ~0.7 for Al alloys (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000043) | Reasonable for KBM/transition regime |
| P_L/d_b = 3333 W/mm in KBM | KBM boundary ~3500 W/mm (pqac-00000062) | Consistent; near HCM/KBM boundary |
| Plume attenuation 0.05–0.2 % | Yb-fibre welding: 11–23 % at 1 atm (pqac-00000035) | Design value may be 1–2 orders low; cross-flow helps but needs measurement |
| 700/900 nm ratio = 2570 K | Pyrometer ratio can be misleading; plume biases ~45 °C on Ni (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000039) | Physically plausible as regime index, not validated as true temperature |
| Si camera threshold ~1170 K | Si/NIR calibrated 600–825 °C; SWIR needed for Al (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000056) | Consistent; confirms Si blindness to mushy zone |
| Coaxial signal uniform across field | 36–51 % uncorrected loss across field (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018) | Major unaddressed issue; per-band calibration essential |
| AE through waveguide adequate | Gas pump noise 10× baseline (pqac-00000058); waveguide adds transfer function complexity | Noise characterization required before build |

The monitoring design is well-conceived in its multi-modal approach and spectral band selection (avoiding galvo-mirror stop bands and atomic emission lines). However, the critical gap is the absence of a spatial calibration strategy for the coaxial channels through the f-theta lens, which published measurements show can introduce errors exceeding the process signatures of interest. The two-colour pyrometer should be treated as a qualitative regime indicator rather than a thermometer until validated against independent measurements. The AE system requires pre-build noise characterization with all machine subsystems running, and the plume attenuation estimate should be revisited given the order-of-magnitude discrepancy with published welding measurements.
"}

{"answer": "## Critical Review of In-Situ Monitoring Design for a Lab-Built LPBF Machine Processing Aluminium Alloys

### (a) Findings Compared with Published Measurements and Practice

**Melt-pool regime and size.** The operating point of 320 W with a 96 µm spot gives P_L/d_b ≈ 3333 W/mm. Leis et al. mapped the AlSi10Mg process window and placed the optimum at P_L/d_b = 3000–3500 W/mm, corresponding to "key-bowl melting" (KBM)—an intermediate regime between heat-conduction melting (HCM, aspect ratio <0.7) and deep-penetration melting (DPM, aspect ratio >1.4) (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000064). The KBM regime features a shallow vapour depression with an aspect ratio near unity—consistent with the design's claim that tracks remain conduction-shaped up to ~350 W while surface boiling begins from ~200 W. The model's calibrated absorptivity of 0.35 sits between the literature values for aluminium alloy conduction-mode absorptivity (~0.15) and transition-mode absorptivity (~0.425), and is therefore physically reasonable for the shallow-depression/KBM regime (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000043). Patel and Vlasea further noted that aluminium alloys have a narrow conduction-to-keyhole transition window because of their high reflectivity, low surface tension at boiling (~0.28 N/m), and volatile Mg content, so the boundary is sensitive to small perturbations in power or focus (pqac-00000005). The modelled pool dimensions (~324 × 208 µm at 25 °C, ~405 × 260 µm at 200 °C) could not be directly validated against the retrieved literature, which reports aspect ratios and cross-sectional areas rather than absolute widths at this exact parameter set. However, the trend of wider pools at elevated preheat is well established, and the simulated width/depth ratios fall in the expected HCM-to-KBM range.

**Two-colour pyrometer reading.** The design's finding that a 700/900 nm ratio pyrometer reads ~2570 K, nearly independent of speed and preheat, is qualitatively consistent with published pyrometry behaviour in LPBF. Gutknecht et al. demonstrated that the two-colour ratio temperature in LPBF can be misleading: near an overhang where excessive energy was physically present, the ratio temperature paradoxically decreased, and would have driven a feedback controller in the wrong direction (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000041). The ratio is not simply the vapour-depression wall temperature. Deisenroth et al. at NIST showed that hot metal vapour, condensate, and ejecta can emit, absorb, reflect, and refract radiation before it reaches the detector, with plume contributions biasing a solidification-temperature measurement by approximately 45 °C (16 °C standard uncertainty) even for well-characterized high-purity nickel (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000009). The design's interpretation that the ratio reads the "depression wall" is therefore an oversimplification. Rather, the signal is a radiance-weighted average over the spatially integrated field of view, dominated by the hottest emitting surface (likely the depression interior), but contaminated by plume emission and selective spectral attenuation. The near-independence from speed and preheat is consistent with the pyrometer being dominated by a hot region whose temperature is set by the boiling point and cavity geometry rather than by bulk thermal conditions—but published evidence cautions that this invariance can break down with changes in plume density, oxide state, or scanning geometry. No published two-colour pyrometry study specifically for aluminium LPBF at these wavelengths was found, so the 2570 K value remains an unvalidated model prediction.

**Silicon camera blindness to Al solidification.** The claim that a 12-bit silicon camera at 850–970 nm cannot see the Al mushy zone (750–925 K, i.e., 477–652 °C) is well supported. Taminger et al. found that a silicon/NIR camera operating at 0.875–1.05 µm was configured for approximately 700–2200 °C and was unsuitable for aluminium's lower temperature range; an InGaAs SWIR camera was specifically required and was calibrated over 300–1000 °C (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055). Boone calibrated a silicon camera with an 850 nm long-pass filter over 600–825 °C (pqac-00000056). These observations confirm that silicon detectors at NIR wavelengths have practical detection thresholds around 600–700 °C for metallic surfaces with low emissivity, placing the Al mushy zone at or below the detection limit. The design's InGaAs channel at 1.55 µm extending sensitivity to ~800 K is therefore a well-motivated addition.

**Spatter reaching cover slides.** The literature confirms that spatter and vapour condensate contaminate optics and powder beds in LPBF (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000032). However, no published study was found that quantifies the fraction of spatter droplets reaching a cover slide at a specific height, so the design's modelled 1.5–5 % fraction reaching a slide 126 mm above the plate is a machine-specific CFD prediction that cannot be directly validated against literature values. The qualitative finding that cross-flow removes most airborne spatter and condensate is consistent with published studies showing that stronger, more uniform gas flow improves spatter removal and reduces redeposition (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

**Thermophoretic deposition.** The design's prediction that a window 10 K colder than the gas collects 20–120× more condensate via thermophoresis is physically plausible but was not found in the LPBF-specific literature. Thermophoresis is well documented in aerosol science and welding fume contexts, but quantitative LPBF window-contamination studies with controlled temperature differentials were not retrieved.

**Plume attenuation.** The design's modelled 0.05–0.2 % beam attenuation appears significantly lower than published measurements. Brown et al. reviewed laser welding plume attenuation and reported total attenuation values of 11–23 % at atmospheric pressure for Yb-fibre laser welding, decreasing to ~2 % at reduced pressures around 3 kPa (pqac-00000035). The dominant mechanism for 1 µm lasers is Rayleigh scattering by ultra-fine condensate particles rather than inverse bremsstrahlung absorption (pqac-00000034). The design's value of 0.05–0.2 % may be reasonable for the aluminium LPBF case at modest power (320 W) with effective cross-flow removing fume, but it is 1–2 orders of magnitude lower than the welding measurements at atmospheric pressure and should be treated as an optimistic lower bound. ### (b) Failure Modes Not Addressed in the Design

**1. Scan-angle-dependent coaxial signal (vignetting and chromatic aberration).** This is the most critical omission. Brandau et al. demonstrated that coaxial monitoring intensity through an F-theta lens dropped by 36 % on solid samples and 51 % on powder-coated samples across the scan field, with only 30.2 % of the reference intensity remaining at 18.5° beam tilt (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019). The Thorlabs FTH160-1064 f-theta lens is designed for 1064 nm laser delivery, not for broadband monitoring. Chromatic aberration shifts the focal position for shorter wavelengths, so the 680–720 nm and 880–920 nm pyrometer bands may have different field-dependent collection efficiencies—corrupting the two-colour ratio spatially across the build plate. Without per-band, per-position calibration, the photodiode pyrometer data will contain systematic spatial errors that could exceed real process variations. A quasi-coaxial approach using reflective optics reduced residual deviation to 1.8 % (pqac-00000017).

**2. Ghost reflections and back-reflections.** Caprio et al. identified internal back-reflections in the coaxial imaging chain as a source of bright artifacts (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000049). The design does not mention shielding, differential sensing, or galvo-synchronous noise characterization. Published monitoring reviews note EMI as a concern for sensitive AE and photodiode measurements in LPBF environments.

**6. Lane et al. at NIST emphasized the importance of reference measurements and uncertainty quantification for LPBF monitoring (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007).

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Discussion of risk ranking rationale:**

Risk 1 (scan-angle dependence) is ranked highest because it affects every coaxial measurement channel continuously and cannot be corrected post-hoc without a spatial calibration. The measured 36–51 % signal variation across the field (pqac-00000018) exceeds many process signatures of interest, which are typically 10–30 % changes in photodiode intensity. Risk 2 (pyrometer misinterpretation) is ranked second because the design explicitly interprets the ~2570 K ratio as a physical temperature of the depression wall. Published evidence shows this interpretation can be qualitatively wrong—the ratio moved in the opposite direction to true energy input near an overhang (pqac-00000039)—and that plume emission biases even well-calibrated single-wavelength measurements by tens of degrees (pqac-00000009). For aluminium, where the plume contains volatile Mg and potentially Na/K with strong atomic emission lines, spectral contamination of the pyrometer bands is a particular concern.

Risk 3 (AE noise) is ranked third because the gas-loop pump noise was measured at 10× the baseline, potentially burying crack signals from hot-cracking-susceptible alloys like 7075 (pqac-00000058). The waveguide coupling adds unknown transfer-function modifications.

Risk 4 (window contamination) is ranked fourth because it creates a time-dependent systematic error that affects all coaxial channels simultaneously but at different rates depending on wavelength-dependent scattering by condensate particles.

Risk 5 (Si camera blindness) is ranked fifth because while confirmed by literature (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000055), the design already acknowledges this limitation and proposes the InGaAs channel as mitigation. The risk is that the InGaAs channel may be deferred as "optional," leaving the Si camera as the only imaging sensor, in which case solidification monitoring for the Al alloys would be impossible.

| Design Claim | Literature Value | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Absorptivity 0.35 | Conduction ~0.15, transition ~0.425, keyhole ~0.7 for Al alloys (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000043) | Reasonable for KBM/transition regime |
| P_L/d_b = 3333 W/mm in KBM | KBM boundary ~3500 W/mm (pqac-00000062) | Consistent; near HCM/KBM boundary |
| Plume attenuation 0.05–0.2 % | Yb-fibre welding: 11–23 % at 1 atm (pqac-00000035) | Design value may be 1–2 orders low; cross-flow helps but needs measurement |
| 700/900 nm ratio = 2570 K | Pyrometer ratio can be misleading; plume biases ~45 °C on Ni (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000039) | Physically plausible as regime index, not validated as true temperature |
| Si camera threshold ~1170 K | Si/NIR calibrated 600–825 °C; SWIR needed for Al (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000056) | Consistent; confirms Si blindness to mushy zone |

Context: a lab-built desktop laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for screening aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, 6061, 7075, grain-refined variants). 500 W single-mode CW fibre laser at 1070 nm into a SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo (up to ~1.1 m/s) and a Thorlabs FTH160-1064 f-theta (f = 160 mm), ~96 um 1/e2 spot; 200-350 W; 30 um layers; plates 25-75 mm across heated to 200 C; argon at ~1 atm with a 2.5-3 m/s cross-flow (200 + 40 L/min) over the plate in a ~280 x 190 x 120 mm chamber. We modelled an in-situ monitoring design and want a critical review against the published literature and practice.

The design and what our models found:
1. Coaxial branch behind a short-pass dichroic (Thorlabs DMSP1000) that reflects 1070 nm into the galvo: a shared short-pass 1070 nm blocker; a second dichroic sends 955-990 nm to a monochrome IMX296 global-shutter camera at 7.4 um per pixel (0.94 x 0.71 mm field, ~500 fps cropped); a third splits a two-colour pair, 680-720 nm and 880-920 nm, onto two Si photodiodes (Thorlabs PDA36A2) behind 500 um pinholes (a 1.6 mm field on the plate); an optional InGaAs channel at 1625-1725 nm, or a coaxial SWIR area camera, to see the pool edge. Bands chosen to avoid the 750-875 nm stop band reported for standard 1064 nm galvo mirror coatings and the Al, Mg, K and Na lines.
2. Melt pool (3D quasi-steady conduction model with a powder layer and enhanced liquid conductivity, absorptivity 0.35 calibrated to measured AlSi10Mg track widths): at 96 um, 320 W, 1.1 m/s the pool is ~324 x 208 um on a 25 C plate and ~405 x 260 um on a 200 C plate; the surface reaches boiling from ~200 W, so a shallow vapour depression forms (transition regime), while measured tracks stay conduction-shaped to ~350 W; the 700/900 nm ratio reads ~2,570 K (the depression wall) almost independent of speed and preheat; a 12-bit silicon camera at 850-970 nm sees only surface above ~1,170 K, so it cannot see the mushy zone (750-925 K), while InGaAs at 1.55 um reaches ~800 K; the mushy zone lasts 22-72 us (AlSi10Mg, 6061) and 67-156 us (7075) at 1.1 m/s, 2-3x longer at 200 C; without skywriting the photodiode signal rises 19-31 % at track ends.
3. Plume, condensate and spatter (OpenFOAM k-omega SST, 285k cells, Lagrangian particles): ~0.47 g of condensate per hour of lasing for AlSi10Mg at 320 W; the cross-flow removes nearly all of it through the outlet; 1.5-5 % of 100-200 um Al spatter droplets reach the laser cover slide 126 mm above the plate still molten; a side window at 13 deg elevation gets at most 0.1 % of spatter; a 1-3 L/min argon purge across that window cuts condensate deposition 13-45x; a window 10 K colder than the gas collects 20-120x more condensate (thermophoresis); the plume attenuates the beam by ~0.05-0.2 %.
4. Side high-speed camera (Kron Chronos 2.1-HD) through a 31 mm port in the side wall at 13 deg elevation, 10-20 us exposures, pulsed 850 nm LED light; a steep second camera through the lid at ~60 deg.
5. Acoustic emission for cracking: a broadband sensor coupled to the plate's underside through a waveguide (or the plate's drawbar) down the hollow piston rod, preamp kept at or below 65 C, digitised at >= 2 MS/s.
6. Timing: the RTC6 scan card as the master clock; photodiodes, AE and the laser gate on one 4-channel digitizer (PicoScope 4444) whose clock is fitted every layer to the recorded laser-gate edges; a 0.25 ms galvo tracking-delay correction; camera triggers from a microcontroller gated by an RTC6 digital output.

Questions:
(a) Which of these findings conflict with published measurements or practice? In particular: the Al melt-pool regime and size at this operating point; whether a 700/900 nm ratio pyrometer on Al reads mainly the vapour depression; whether silicon cameras are effectively blind to Al solidification; how much spatter reaches cover slides; thermophoretic deposition on cooler windows; the plume attenuation.
(b) What failure modes have others hit with similar coaxial, off-axis and acoustic monitoring that this design does not address? For example scan-angle-dependent signal (vignetting) and its correction, ghost reflections and back-reflection into the coaxial path, thermal drift of dichroics and filters, emissivity changes with oxide, EMI from galvo and servo drives, AE noise from the recoater and gas loop, calibration drift, data volume.
(c) Rank the five biggest risks to getting useful data from this design and suggest the cheapest experiment to retire each.
Give quantitative evidence and sources.

Use battery power or isolation temporarily to identify EMI, and reject the installation if pump-on lead-break SNR is inadequate in the intended **50–600 kHz** band. |
| 4 | Cover-slide/window contamination creates time-dependent optical drift | Literature confirms that vapour condensate deposits on process surfaces and optics, that gas flow is needed to transport fume and spatter, and that window contamination can reduce delivered and detected radiation; however, it does **not** substantiate a universal **1.5–5%** fraction of droplets reaching a cover slide. The predicted fraction and the modeled **13–45× purge benefit** are therefore machine-specific hypotheses requiring measurement (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000032). | Install pre-weighed witness coupons beside the cover slide and side window, plus a fixed LED transmission path through each window. Run short, equal laser-on-dose builds with purge **off/on** and window temperatures matched, colder and warmer than the gas. Measure transmission, mass gain and microscope particle coverage versus laser-on time. This simultaneously tests spatter arrival, condensate accumulation, purge effectiveness and the claimed thermophoretic enhancement. |
| 5 | Silicon camera cannot observe Al solidification/mushy-zone geometry | A silicon/NIR system operating around **0.875–1.05 µm** was configured for roughly **700–2200 °C**, whereas an InGaAs SWIR camera was calibrated over about **300–1000 °C** and was the only tested camera capable of measuring lower temperatures relevant to aluminium. Thus Al mushy temperatures of approximately **477–652 °C** are at or below a practical silicon-camera range, although the exact cutoff depends on emissivity, optics, exposure and noise rather than wavelength alone (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055). | View an emissivity-characterized heated Al coupon through the complete installed optical path using the intended exposures and gains. Step through **450–900 °C**, record SNR and derive the temperature at which SNR reaches 5. Repeat with controlled oxide states. If silicon cannot meet SNR at solidus, use it only for the hot core/spatter and perform one simultaneous Si–InGaAs single-track trial before purchasing a full SWIR system. |


*Table: The five highest risks are ranked by their likelihood of producing plausible but misleading LPBF monitoring data. Each is paired with a low-cost experiment that provides a quantitative acceptance test before full system integration.*

**Discussion of risk ranking rationale:**

Risk 1 (scan-angle dependence) is ranked highest because it affects every coaxial measurement channel continuously and cannot be corrected post-hoc without a spatial calibration. The measured 36–51 % signal variation across the field (pqac-00000018) exceeds many process signatures of interest, which are typically 10–30 % changes in photodiode intensity. For the two-colour pyrometer, differential chromatic aberration between 700 nm and 900 nm through the f-theta lens could corrupt the ratio itself, not just its amplitude, making flat-field correction insufficient without per-band calibration.

Risk 2 (pyrometer misinterpretation) is ranked second because the design explicitly interprets the ~2570 K ratio as a physical temperature of the depression wall. Published evidence shows this interpretation can be qualitatively wrong—the ratio moved in the opposite direction to true energy input near an overhang (pqac-00000039)—and that plume emission biases even well-calibrated single-wavelength measurements by tens of degrees (pqac-00000009). For aluminium, where the plume contains volatile Mg and potentially Na/K with strong atomic emission lines, spectral contamination of the pyrometer bands is a particular concern.

Risk 3 (AE noise) is ranked third because the gas-loop pump noise was measured at 10× the baseline, potentially burying crack signals from hot-cracking-susceptible alloys like 7075 (pqac-00000058). The waveguide coupling adds unknown transfer-function modifications.

Risk 4 (window contamination) is ranked fourth because it creates a time-dependent systematic error that affects all coaxial channels simultaneously but at different rates depending on wavelength-dependent scattering by condensate particles.

Risk 5 (Si camera blindness) is ranked fifth because while confirmed by literature (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000055), the design already acknowledges this limitation and proposes the InGaAs channel as mitigation. The risk is that the InGaAs channel may be deferred as "optional," leaving the Si camera as the only imaging sensor, in which case solidification monitoring for the Al alloys would be impossible.

### Summary of Key Quantitative Comparisons

| Design Claim | Literature Value | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Absorptivity 0.35 | Conduction ~0.15, transition ~0.425, keyhole ~0.7 for Al alloys (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000043) | Reasonable for KBM/transition regime |
| P_L/d_b = 3333 W/mm in KBM | KBM boundary ~3500 W/mm (pqac-00000062) | Consistent; near HCM/KBM boundary |
| Plume attenuation 0.05–0.2 % | Yb-fibre welding: 11–23 % at 1 atm (pqac-00000035) | Design value may be 1–2 orders low; cross-flow helps but needs measurement |
| 700/900 nm ratio = 2570 K | Pyrometer ratio can be misleading; plume biases ~45 °C on Ni (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000039) | Physically plausible as regime index, not validated as true temperature |
| Si camera threshold ~1170 K | Si/NIR calibrated 600–825 °C; SWIR needed for Al (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000056) | Consistent; confirms Si blindness to mushy zone |
| Coaxial signal uniform across field | 36–51 % uncorrected loss across field (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018) | Major unaddressed issue; per-band calibration essential |
| AE through waveguide adequate | Gas pump noise 10× baseline (pqac-00000058); waveguide adds transfer function complexity | Noise characterization required before build |

The monitoring design is well-conceived in its multi-modal approach and spectral band selection (avoiding galvo-mirror stop bands and atomic emission lines). However, the critical gap is the absence of a spatial calibration strategy for the coaxial channels through the f-theta lens, which published measurements show can introduce errors exceeding the process signatures of interest. The two-colour pyrometer should be treated as a qualitative regime indicator rather than a thermometer until validated against independent measurements. The AE system requires pre-build noise characterization with all machine subsystems running, and the plume attenuation estimate should be revisited given the order-of-magnitude discrepancy with published welding measurements.

contexts.context: The excerpt explains that a two-colour pyrometer calculates a ratio temperature from the relative emitted intensities at two wavelengths. This is not necessarily the true thermodynamic temperature: it depends on assumptions about the target’s spectral emissivity, commonly a wavelength-independent graybody assumption, and on calibration. Two-colour measurements can tolerate emissivity changes or optical-path losses when those effects influence both wavelengths equally, but their uncertainty is difficult to establish without independent reference data. The excerpt does not specifically determine whether the measured temperature corresponds to the vapour-depression wall temperature. It instead warns that LPBF process by-products—including hot metal vapour, condensate, and ejecta—can emit, absorb, reflect, and refract radiation before it reaches the detector. Consequently, the pyrometer reading may be influenced by radiation from or attenuation through these by-products rather than solely by the depression wall. Their contribution varies with laser power, scan velocity, material properties, oxygen content, and shielding-gas velocity, creating process-dependent measurement uncertainty. The provided text does not report the specific trend of ratio temperature versus scan speed and power; it only indicates that these parameters can change by-product effects and therefore potentially alter pyrometry readings.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide a percentage of spatter reaching the cover slide or laser window, a quantitative amount of condensate or fume deposited on optics, or a measured attenuation of the laser beam by the plume. It does, however, describe the qualitative role of cross-flow and chamber-flow design in removing spatter and other process by-products. Gas flow is used to clear the process zone, and lower protective-gas velocity reduces spatter-removal efficiency. A steady, uniform, high-velocity flow over the powder bed improves removal and can improve final part quality. The positions and dimensions of gas inlets and outlets affect flow velocity, uniformity, and spatter concentration. Structural optimization can make the flow field more uniform and improve its ability to entrain spatter. A redesigned gas-flow system increased spatter removal by reducing the Coanda effect, while additional nozzles further supported removal. The excerpt also notes that streamlined flow channels can reduce outlet vortices and prevent the vapor plume and spatters from redepositing on the forming surface. These findings support the conclusion that stronger, more uniform, properly directed cross-flow reduces spatter transport and redeposition, but no numerical optics-contamination or laser-attenuation values are reported here.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative information about plume-related laser attenuation and spatter generation in laser powder bed fusion, but it does not report the requested percentage of spatter reaching a cover slide or laser window, the quantity of condensate or fume deposited on optics, a numerical attenuation percentage, or the effect of cross-flow on removal. It states that increasing laser energy can drive keyhole-mode melting, whose unstable cavity may entrap gas bubbles and increase spatter ejection, contributing to porosity. Metal vapor and cover gas above the melt pool can form an ionized plasma plume, and the plume attenuates the laser beam, reducing delivered energy. Three attenuation mechanisms are identified: inverse bremsstrahlung absorption through electron–photon interactions, Rayleigh scattering by plume particles, and beam refraction that increases the effective laser spot size. The excerpt indicates that atmosphere manipulation can reduce these attenuation mechanisms and thereby reduce defects. It also lists cover-gas properties, including ionization energies and thermal conductivities, which are relevant to plume behavior. However, the supplied pages do not discuss optical-window contamination, condensate/fume deposition rates, spatter transport percentages, or cross-flow conditions and removal efficiency; those details would need to be obtained from later sections or other sources.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides partial background relevant to coaxial melt-pool monitoring in LPBF, but it does not explicitly enumerate the requested failure modes or describe a correction method for scan-angle dependence. It explains that coaxial monitoring shares the laser’s optical path and relies on a dichroic mirror or beam splitter to separate the approximately 1070 nm laser from the melt-pool’s radiant emission. This shared-path arrangement introduces complex optical integration and makes the system vulnerable to contamination of optical components. The excerpt also notes that coaxial systems require simultaneous acquisition of laser-position data to register measurements to locations in the build, and that their data processing involves more complex algorithms. These issues could be relevant when diagnosing angle-dependent signal variation or optical artifacts, but the passage does not specifically discuss scan-angle-dependent vignetting, ghost reflections, back-reflection into the laser, thermal drift of dichroic filters, or emissivity changes caused by oxide formation on aluminum. It likewise does not state how scan-angle dependence is corrected—such as through angular calibration, flat-field correction, reference measurements, or model-based compensation. Therefore, the excerpt supports only the general optical architecture and associated integration, contamination, registration, and processing considerations.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several limitations and potential failure mechanisms in coaxial LPBF melt-pool monitoring. Internal back-reflections in the imaging chain can generate bright artifacts and interfere with interpretation of the melt-pool signal; coherent coaxial illumination can additionally produce speckle formation. Signal-processing leakage can cause errors in identifying melt-pool oscillation frequencies, particularly when neighboring spectral peaks lie within the narrow bandwidth of the power-spectral-density estimate. The text also contrasts coaxial/Lagrangian observation with fixed off-axis observation: coaxial monitoring uses a moving observation frame and therefore removes acquisition-time constraints associated with a fixed viewpoint, while frequency resolution remains governed by the observed scan-vector length, with Δfres,PD = v/lobs. The excerpt does not explicitly discuss scan-angle-dependent signal vignetting, ghost reflections, back-reflection into the process laser, thermal drift of dichroic filters, or emissivity changes caused by oxide formation on aluminum. Nor does it provide a specific scan-angle correction algorithm. Its relevant design guidance is to use coaxial illumination for more uniform illumination and lower power consumption, while recognizing internal reflections and speckle as disadvantages; off-axis illumination is easier to set up but may suffer from nonuniform illumination and requires high intensity over a large area.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates a strong angular and scan-position dependence in coaxial LPBF monitoring. As beam or field tilt increases, the measured spectral intensity decreases. At the maximum tested beam tilt of 18.5°, the coaxial measurement retained only 30.2% of the intensity measured near the reference position, implying a substantial galvo-angle-dependent signal loss. The F-theta lens contributes through both longitudinal and transverse chromatic aberration: because it is not apochromatic, different wavelengths are focused at different axial positions, increasing the effective integration zone and reducing the contribution of unfocused wavelengths. Across the scan field, the shorter-wavelength (blue) component has a shorter focal length, so at larger field angles the monitoring point can move away from the interaction zone; the shorter-wavelength spectral integral consequently decreases. At nonzero material and beam tilt, projection also enlarges the focus spot and lowers laser intensity, although the excerpt identifies chromatic aberration as the more important influence. A quasi-coaxial arrangement using a second scanner and reflective mirror optics avoids wavelength-dependent transmission errors. Its field-dependent spot-size and numerical-aperture variations are corrected using a white-light reference measurement and a 100-μm optical fiber scanned across the processing field, reducing the remaining intensity deviation to a maximum of 1.8%.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that coaxial monitoring intensity depends on scan position and trajectory because the meltpool and its thermal tail change their orientation and position relative to the coaxial sensor’s field of view. During straight scanning, the emitting region has a relatively stable geometry, but during sharp scan-direction changes—especially 180° turnarounds—the scan velocity and direction change rapidly. This changes the fraction of the meltpool and heated surroundings captured by the sensor. A meltpool tail that is partly outside the effective measurement field during straight scanning may contribute differently during a turnaround, producing intensity changes unrelated to actual meltpool-depth or energy-input changes. Therefore, cumulative coaxial emission intensity has a geometric/angular dependence and may be ambiguous during transient scan paths. However, the provided excerpt does not quantify the signal variation as a function of galvo angle, does not discuss the optical effect of an f-theta lens, and does not identify specific corrections or calibration formulas applied to compensate for these effects. contexts.context: In LPBF, the coaxial monitoring signal is strongly position-dependent because the scan position changes the laser/workpiece incidence angle through the F-theta scanning optics. Signal intensity decreases as the galvo angle and distance from the scan-field center increase. Across the working field, the uncorrected spectral intensity falls by approximately 36% for solid samples and 51% for powder-coated samples, with the larger powder decrease attributed to stronger angle-dependent effects. The F-theta lens also introduces chromatic aberration in the coaxial optical path: short-wavelength components below 510 nm are not detected even at a scanner-mirror angle of 5°. The reported angular dependence is associated with changes in spot size and interaction-zone geometry, as well as the field-dependent numerical aperture and process-radiation geometry. A reflective quasi-coaxial setup avoids the severe short-wave loss and records the process signal accurately. For solid materials, field measurements can be normalized using correction factors incorporating the measuring channel’s numerical aperture and laser intensity distribution over the working field. The correction can adjust the overall spectral intensity, but it cannot independently restore individual atomic emission peaks; residual deviations arise from setup geometry and the field-dependent emission angle.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes several LPBF acoustic-emission monitoring considerations. Sensor location strongly affects signal strength, while noise sources reduce measurement accuracy. PZT sensors are widely preferred because of their stability and cost-effectiveness; mounting them directly on or beneath the substrate provides comprehensive process signals. Good coupling requires a suitable coupling agent and constant clamping force, and thresholding and parameter analysis help distinguish genuine AE events from noise. PZT sensors should be calibrated with standard AE sources, such as a broken lead, to improve acquisition accuracy and repeatability. In PBF/LPBF systems, sensor-cable routing must avoid interference with the powder recoater. The review proposes machining a recess beneath the build platform for the sensor and providing a dedicated cable channel. The excerpt does not specify LPBF recoater-noise characteristics, gas-flow noise, background noise levels, waveguide coupling for LPBF, AE-sensor or preamplifier temperature limits, sampling-rate requirements, or quantitative crack-detection capability. It only notes that PZT AE sensors convert elastic stress waves generated by damage, including crack propagation, into electrical signals. Waveguides and water cooling are discussed primarily for high-temperature DED, especially WA-DED, rather than LPBF. Wavelet denoising, homomorphic deconvolution, and local-least-squares digital filters are reported as effective for improving signal quality in LB-PBF and related processes.

contexts.context: The excerpt distinguishes structure-borne acoustic emission (SBAE) from air-borne acoustic emission (ABAE) monitoring in LPBF. SBAE uses piezoceramic transducers coupled directly to the workpiece and detects vibrations propagating through the solid; ABAE uses microphones or remote sensors and detects signals propagating through air. Air has greater acoustic damping, so SBAE can provide a broader frequency spectrum, whereas ABAE is advantageous for non-contact and remote monitoring. A major practical limitation of SBAE is reproducible sensor coupling: sensors must be reattached when the workpiece changes. The excerpt also describes an indirect coupling arrangement in which a piezo sensor was attached to the sample holder rather than the sample, classifying it as ABAE-type monitoring. Noise reduction and signal processing included wavelet packet analysis, selection of frequency-band energies, denoising, and machine-learning classification. In an LPBF study, a remotely positioned optical microphone captured airborne emissions from 10 Hz to 1 MHz, synchronized with X-ray imaging at 10 kHz. Acoustic monitoring was used to identify process-regime transitions, keyhole behavior, pore formation, and potentially defect-related material damage, including cracks or microfractures. However, the excerpt does not provide specific information on recoater noise, gas-flow noise, quantitative background-noise levels, waveguide coupling, sensor or preamplifier temperature limits, or dedicated crack-detection performance.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes plume or metal-vapour attenuation in LPBF as the reduction in laser energy delivered to the melt pool when metal vapour and surrounding cover gas interact with the laser beam. The vapour and gas can become ionized, forming a plasma plume above the melt pool. Attenuation occurs through three principal mechanisms: inverse bremsstrahlung absorption, in which electrons and photons interact; Rayleigh scattering by plume particles; and refraction, which increases the beam’s effective spot size. The extent of these interactions depends on laser wavelength and power, as well as the ionization energies of the metal vapour and cover gas. Metal vapours are more readily ionized than common cover gases, with listed ionization energies of 7.9 eV for iron, 6.8 eV for titanium, and 6.0 eV for aluminum. The excerpt does not provide a measured percentage of laser power lost specifically to plume absorption and scattering, nor does it report direct beam-attenuation measurements. The percentages stated concern melt-pool coupling rather than plume loss: conduction-mode melting typically absorbs less than 30% of incident laser energy, while keyhole-mode melting can absorb as much as 90% because of repeated absorption within the depression. Therefore, these values should not be interpreted as the percentage lost to plume attenuation.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes plume and vaporization effects in LPBF qualitatively, but it does not report a measured plume-induced attenuation of the laser beam or a percentage of laser power lost through plume absorption and scattering. Increasing energy density increases metal vaporization; the resulting plume becomes larger and is associated with increased quality loss. Vaporization by-products, including plume and spatter, can interfere with the laser path. In particular, insufficient dust-removal airflow allows steady-state turbulence and plume to form above the molding chamber, which “seriously blocks the laser.” Adequate circulating airflow can remove the plume, whereas excessive airflow may disturb the powder and distort the molding state. The excerpt also notes that atmospheric composition affects plume/spatter behavior: helium reduced spatter relative to argon, although helium produced more severe ablation and greater energy loss. These observations establish that plume attenuation depends on vaporization intensity, airflow, and shielding-gas atmosphere, but the supplied pages provide no direct optical measurements, attenuation coefficient, transmission value, or percentage loss of incident laser power. A quantitative answer would require a dedicated beam-transmission or power-measurement study conducted during metal processing.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports measurements of laser-beam attenuation by the plasma or metal-vapour plume during laser processing, primarily for Yb-fiber and CO2 laser welding rather than LPBF specifically. At approximately atmospheric pressure (101 kPa), measured total attenuation through the plume ranges from about 11% to 23%, implying that this fraction of incident laser power is lost through plume-related effects overall. One Yb-fiber welding measurement found an average attenuation of 23% at 101 kPa, decreasing to only 2% at 3 kPa. Across three studies, attenuation fell below 5% at 20 kPa. The excerpt attributes attenuation mainly to absorption and scattering by the plasma plume, while also noting that plume-induced refraction can shift and destabilize the effective laser spot; this is a beam-delivery effect distinct from power loss. A pressure threshold between 20 and 10 kPa was reported, below which plume absorption and scattering were greatly reduced. Reduced pressure also decreased plume generation, increased penetration, and improved beam stability. Hyperbaric processing produced the opposite trend: increased pressure intensified and prolonged the plume, increased attenuation, and yielded shallower melt pools. These values provide relevant comparative measurements for plume attenuation, but the excerpt does not give a dedicated LPBF-specific percentage.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not establish that the two-colour pyrometer measures the temperature inside a vapour depression. It describes the ratio temperature as a measurement derived from two photodetector channels and intended to represent the emitting melt-pool surface temperature, assuming suitable emissivity behaviour. Changes in ratio can arise from true temperature changes, selective attenuation, or unequal emissivity changes, so ratio temperature should not automatically be interpreted as an accurate thermodynamic temperature under all LPBF conditions.
